files.README.md:
# Freelance Services Page Kit

Most freelance websites list skills ("branding, web design, UX") and hope the right client works out the rest. The right client usually doesn't. This kit walks you through writing a services page that tells one specific kind of client exactly what you do, what it costs, how it works and why you, so the good ones get in touch and the poor fits filter themselves out.

You'll end with a finished page you can paste into any website builder, a portfolio platform, a PDF or a proposal.

## What's inside

| File | What it's for |
|---|---|
| `client-research.md` | Gather the words your best clients actually use (the raw material for everything else) |
| `package-builder.md` | Turn "I do everything" into two or three clear packages with prices |
| `page-template.md` | The page, section by section, with fill-in prompts and rules for each section |
| `worked-example.md` | A complete, finished services page for a fictional freelancer, with notes |
| `headline-bank.md` | Twelve headline patterns, with examples, to get unstuck fast |
| `objection-faq.md` | The questions clients worry about but rarely ask, with answer templates |
| `word-swaps.csv` | 40 vague phrases and specific replacements |
| `review-checklist.md` | A 20-point check before you publish, plus a five-second test to run on a friend |

## How to use it (about 3 hours, in two sittings)

**Sitting 1: research and offer (90 min)**

1. Fill in `client-research.md` (45 min). Don't skip this: it's where the good lines come from.
2. Work through `package-builder.md` (45 min). You'll end with your packages and starting prices.

**Sitting 2: write and check (90 min)**

3. Draft the page with `page-template.md`, keeping `worked-example.md` open beside it (60 min). Use `headline-bank.md` and `objection-faq.md` when you get stuck.
4. Run every sentence through `word-swaps.csv`, then go through `review-checklist.md` (30 min).

## Who this is for

- Freelancers whose website gets visitors but few enquiries
- Freelancers who get enquiries, but mostly from the wrong clients or the wrong budget
- New freelancers writing their first services page
- Anyone rewriting a page that says "I'm passionate about..."

## Honest expectations

A clear services page makes it much easier for interested people to say yes, and for poor fits to self-select out. It won't create traffic on its own; pair it with the places your clients already find you (referrals, a profile, outreach). Rewrite it once a year, or whenever your best clients change.

# Client Research Worksheet

The best services pages sound like the client, not the freelancer. This worksheet collects your clients' own words. You'll lift phrases straight from here into your headline, intro and FAQ.

Time: about 45 minutes.

## Part 1: Pick your best three clients

"Best" means: you did great work, they paid well and on time, and you'd happily do it again. If you're new, use the three people you'd most like to work for, or the three projects you're proudest of.

| | Client 1 | Client 2 | Client 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Who they are (role, type of business, size) | | | |
| What they hired you for | | | |
| Roughly what they paid | | | |
| How they found you | | | |

**What do they have in common?** Write one sentence:

> My best clients are [type of person/business] who need [outcome] because [trigger].

## Part 2: Mine their words

Go through your emails, enquiry forms, call notes and any thank-you messages from these clients. Copy exact phrases, typos and all. You're looking for:

**The trigger: what made them go looking for help?**
(Examples: "we're launching in June", "our old site is embarrassing", "I've been putting this off for a year")

- 
- 
- 

**The pain: how they described the problem.**
(Examples: "nobody can find anything on our site", "I don't have time to write", "the last designer disappeared")

- 
-

**The fear: what they were worried about when hiring.**
(Examples: "I don't know how much this should cost", "I don't want to be locked into something", "I'm not techy")

- 
- 
- 

**The win: what they said after.**
(Examples: "I finally send people to our site without apologising", "it saved me every Friday afternoon")

- 
-

## Part 3: If you don't have enough material, ask

Send this to two or three past clients. Most are happy to help, and you'll often get a testimonial out of it too.

> Hi [name],
>
> I'm rewriting how I describe my work, and you're exactly the kind of client I'd love more of. Would you mind answering three quick questions? A sentence each is perfect.
>
> 1. What was going on that made you look for help with [project]?
> 2. What almost stopped you hiring someone?
> 3. What's different now?
>
> Thanks so much,
> [your name]

(Only use their answers as a testimonial on your page if they say yes to that specifically. Use their real words, unchanged.)

## Part 4: Summarise

| Question | Your answer (use their words where you can) |
|---|---|
| Who is the page for? | |
| What triggers them to look for help? | |
| What's the problem in their words? | |
| What are they afraid of? | |
| What does "done" look like for them? | |
| What do you do that others in your field often don't? | |

Keep this table open while you write. Every section of the page should answer one of these rows.

# Package Builder

A list of skills makes the client do the work of figuring out what to buy. Packages do that work for them: a named bundle, a clear outcome, a price or starting price, and a timeline.

Time: about 45 minutes.

## Step 1: List what clients actually buy

Look at your last 5 to 10 projects. What did people pay for? Write them down as outcomes, not skills.

| Project | Skill-language (how you'd describe it) | Outcome-language (what the client got) | Price | Time taken |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |

Example row: "Web design, WordPress" becomes "A 5-page site the owner can update herself", $2,400, 3 weeks.

## Step 2: Group them into two or three packages

Most freelancers land on a version of this:

| Package type | What it is | Why it's useful |
|---|---|---|
| **Starter** | A small, fixed piece of work, often a diagnosis, audit or plan | Low-risk first purchase; many clients upgrade later |
| **Core** | The thing most of your best clients buy | Where most of your income comes from; make it the obvious choice |
| **Ongoing** | A monthly arrangement after the core work | Steady income for you, continuity for them |

You don't need all three. Two clear packages beat four fuzzy ones.

## Step 3: Define each package

Fill in one block per package.

```
Package name:            [plain and descriptive, e.g. "Website Refresh", not "Gold"]
Who it's for:            [one sentence]
The outcome:             [what's true for them when it's done]
What's included:         [3-7 bullet points, concrete]
What's not included:     [1-3 bullet points; prevents scope creep]
Timeline:                [e.g. 3 weeks from kickoff]
Price:                   [fixed / from $X / $X per month]
What happens next:       [how they start]
```

## Step 4: Set prices you'll actually say out loud

- **Start from what you've charged.** Look at the prices in step 1. Your core package should be close to the typical price of your best projects, not your cheapest.
- **Show prices or a "from" price.** Clients are often nervous about cost. A "from $X" price answers the biggest unasked question and filters out budgets that don't fit. If you really can't show any price, say what affects the price and give a typical range.
- **Make the gap sensible.** A starter at roughly a fifth to a third of the core price is a comfortable first step.
- **Round numbers are fine.** Odd prices like $2,397 can feel like a sales trick for professional services.

## Worked example

Maya is a freelance web developer working mainly with local service businesses (physiotherapists, accountants, small clinics).

**Package 1: Website Check-up**
- Who it's for: owners who suspect their site is losing them enquiries but don't know why
- Outcome: a clear, prioritised list of what to fix, and what it would cost
- Included: 60-minute call, review of the site on phone and desktop, speed and basic search check, a written report with the top 10 fixes ranked by impact
- Not included: making the fixes
- Timeline: 1 week
- Price: $350 (credited against a Website Refresh if booked within 60 days)

**Package 2: Website Refresh**
- Who it's for: established local businesses with an outdated site
- Outcome: a modern, fast site of up to 8 pages that the owner can update without help
- Included: plan and page structure, design, build, writing help for key pages, contact and booking set-up, a recorded training session, 30 days of fixes after launch
- Not included: photography, ongoing content writing, online shop
- Timeline: 4 to 5 weeks
- Price: from $3,800

**Package 3: Care Plan**
- Who it's for: Refresh clients who'd rather not think about their website
- Included: updates and backups, up to 2 hours of changes a month, a quarterly check-in
- Price: $180 per month, cancel any time with 30 days' notice

# Services Page Template

Fill in each section in order. Each one has a job, a fill-in prompt and rules. Aim for 600 to 1,000 words in total: long enough to answer real questions, short enough to read on a phone.

---

## Section 1: Headline and opening (the five-second section)

**Its job:** tell the right visitor, in five seconds, that they're in the right place.

**Fill in:**

> **Headline:** [Outcome] for [specific client].
>
> **Subheading:** I [what you do] so you can [what changes for them], without [the thing they fear].
>
> **Button:** [See packages and prices] / [Book a 20-minute call]

**Rules:**
- Name the client. "For local clinics" beats "for businesses".
- Name the outcome, not the skill. "Websites that bring in bookings" beats "Web design".
- No "passionate", "creative solutions" or "elevate your brand". See `word-swaps.csv`.
- Stuck? Use `headline-bank.md`.

---

## Section 2: "Does this sound familiar?" (the problem)

**Its job:** prove you understand their situation, in their words.

**Fill in:** three to five short bullet points, taken from the "pain" and "trigger" rows in `client-research.md`.

> You might be here because:
> - [pain in their words]
> - [trigger in their words]
> - [frustration in their words]

**Rules:**
- Use their language, not industry terms.
- Keep it short. You're showing you understand, not dwelling on the problem.

---

## Section 3: What I do (the packages)

**Its job:** make choosing easy.

**Fill in:** one block per package from `package-builder.md`.

> ### [Package name]
> **For:** [who]
> **You get:** [outcome in one sentence]
> - [included item]
> - [included item]
> - [included item]
>
> **Timeline:** [X weeks] · **Price:** [from $X]
> [Button: Start with a [package name]]

**Rules:**
- Put your core package in the middle or mark it "Most popular" only if it actually is.
- Show prices or "from" prices if you possibly can.
- Include "not included" in your proposal, not here, unless it's a common misunderstanding.

---

## Section 4: How it works (the process)

**Its job:** remove the fear of the unknown. Nervous clients want to know what happens after they click.

**Fill in:** three to five numbered steps.

> 1. **[Step name].** [What happens, what they need to do, how long it takes.]
> 2. ...

**Rules:**
- Say what the client has to do at each step, not just what you do.
- Include how long things take.

---

## Section 5: Why me (the proof)

**Its job:** answer "why you and not someone cheaper or more famous?"

**Fill in:**

> - **[Specific experience]:** e.g. "I've built sites for 14 physiotherapy clinics, so I already know what your patients look for."
> - **[Specific way of working]:** e.g. "You'll always deal with me, not a junior."
> - **[Evidence]:** a real result, a case study link, or a real testimonial used with permission.

**Rules:**
- Specific beats impressive. "14 clinics" beats "years of experience".
- Only claim what you can back up. Never invent testimonials, numbers or client names.
- If you're new, use your process, your relevant background and your guarantee instead of volume.

---

## Section 6: Questions (the objections)

**Its job:** answer the worries people won't ask out loud.

**Fill in:** four to six questions from `objection-faq.md`.

---

## Section 7: Next step (the call to action)

**Its job:** make getting in touch feel small and safe.

**Fill in:**

> **[Ready to [outcome]?]**
> [Book a free 20-minute call / Send me a short message] and I'll [what happens next, e.g. reply within one working day with honest advice on which package fits, or whether I'm not the right person].
> [Button]

**Rules:**
- One clear action. Not a call, a form, a newsletter and social links all at once.
- Say when they'll hear back.
- Offering to tell them if you're not the right fit builds a lot of trust.

---

## Before you publish

Go through `review-checklist.md`.
files.worked-example.md:
# Worked Example: A Finished Services Page

Maya is a fictional freelance web developer who works with local service businesses. Below is her finished page, built with `page-template.md` and the packages from `package-builder.md`. Notes in *italics* explain the choices; they're not part of the page.

---

# Websites that bring in bookings, for local clinics and practices

I build simple, fast websites for physiotherapists, dentists, accountants and other local practices, so new clients can find you, trust you and book, without you having to learn web design.

**[See packages and prices]**

*Note: the headline names the outcome (bookings) and the client (local clinics and practices). The subheading adds the fear ("without you having to learn web design"), which came straight from her client research.*

---

## Does this sound familiar?

- You send people to your website and then apologise for it
- Patients phone to ask things that should be on the site, like your hours or whether you take their insurance
- Your last web person stopped replying, and nobody knows the password
- You know you should "do something about the website", and it's been on the list for a year

*Note: every bullet is a paraphrase of something a real client said to her. The third one is the most common fear she hears.*

---

## Packages

### Website Check-up
**For:** owners who suspect their site is losing them enquiries but don't know why.
**You get:** a clear, ranked list of what to fix and what it would cost.
- 60-minute call about your business and your clients
- Review of your site on phone and desktop
- Speed and basic search check
- Written report: your top 10 fixes, ranked by impact

**Timeline:** 1 week · **Price:** $350, credited against a Website Refresh booked within 60 days

### Website Refresh
**For:** established practices with a site that's out of date.
**You get:** a modern site of up to 8 pages that you can update yourself.
- Page plan built around what your clients ask most
- Design and build, fast on phones
- Help writing your key pages
- Contact and online booking set up
- A recorded training session, so you're never stuck
- 30 days of fixes after launch

**Timeline:** 4 to 5 weeks · **Price:** from $3,800

### Care Plan
**For:** Refresh clients who'd rather not think about their website.
- Updates and backups
- Up to 2 hours of changes each month
- A quarterly check-in on what's working

**Price:** $180/month, cancel with 30 days' notice

*Note: plain names, real prices. The Check-up gives cautious clients a small first step, and the credit gives them a reason to continue.*

---

## How it works

1. **Free 20-minute call.** We talk about your practice and what's not working. I'll tell you which package fits, or if you don't need me at all.
2. **Plan (week 1).** I send a one-page plan and a fixed quote. You approve it before anything is billed.
3. **Design and build (weeks 2 to 4).** You see the design early and get two rounds of changes. I'll need your logo, photos and about 2 hours of your time over the month.
4. **Launch and training (week 5).** We go live together, and I show you how to update hours, prices and team details.
5. **30 days of fixes.** Anything that's not right, I fix at no charge.

*Note: step 3 tells the client what they need to do and how much of their time it will take. That's the question busy owners worry about most.*

---

## Why work with me

- **I only work with local practices.** I already know what your clients look for: hours, location, prices, who they'll see, and how to book.
- **You'll always deal with me.** No account managers, no handing you over to a junior.
- **You own everything.** The domain, the site and the passwords are in your name from day one.

> [A short quote from a real client, in their own words, with their name and practice, used with their permission.]

*Note: the testimonial slot is only for a real quote from a real client who agreed to be named. If you don't have one yet, leave this out; the three specific points carry the section.*

---

## Questions

**How much will it really cost?**
The Refresh starts at $3,800 for up to 8 pages with booking set up. The fixed price is in your plan before you commit, and it doesn't change unless you ask for something new.

**I'm not technical. Will I be able to update it?**
Yes. That's what the training session is for, and you keep the recording. Most clients update their hours and team page themselves within the first week.

**What if I don't like the design?**
You see it early and get two rounds of changes before anything is built.

**Do I have to sign up for the Care Plan?**
No. It's optional, and you can cancel with 30 days' notice.

**What happens to my current site?**
It stays up until the new one is ready, and I'll make sure your existing links still work.

---

## Ready to stop apologising for your website?

Book a free 20-minute call. I'll give you honest advice on what to fix first, even if that's something you can do yourself.

**[Book a call]**

I reply to every message within one working day.

---

## Why this page works

- A clinic owner knows in five seconds that it's for them.
- Every price, timeline and next step is on the page, so the call starts with "which package?" instead of "how much?"
- The process section answers "what do I have to do?"
- The FAQ handles cost, skill and commitment, the three things that stop people getting in touch.
- It's about 750 words: easy to read on a phone in three minutes.
files.headline-bank.md:
# Headline Bank

Twelve patterns for the top of your services page. Write five or six options, read them aloud, and pick the one that a client would most likely say back to you in their own words.

| # | Pattern | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | [Outcome] for [client] | Websites that bring in bookings, for local clinics |
| 2 | [Outcome] without [fear] | Brand photography for small shops, without the awkward posing |
| 3 | I help [client] [achieve outcome] | I help early-stage software teams write docs their users actually read |
| 4 | [Deliverable] for [client] who [situation] | Bookkeeping for designers who'd rather be designing |
| 5 | From [before] to [after] | From a messy spreadsheet to a dashboard your team checks every morning |
| 6 | The [role] for [client] | The video editor for coaches who film on their phone |
| 7 | [Outcome] in [timeframe] | A finished pitch deck in two weeks, ready for investors |
| 8 | [Client], [benefit statement] | Independent cafés: menus that make the specials sell |
| 9 | Stop [pain]. Start [gain]. | Stop rewriting the same emails. Start sending ones that get replies. |
| 10 | [Outcome], done for you | Your product listings, written and optimised, done for you |
| 11 | [Number] [thing] for [client] | Illustrations for children's book authors, from sketch to print-ready files |
| 12 | Question headline | Is your website sending clients to your competitors? |

## Rules of thumb

- **Name the client.** If your headline would fit any freelancer in your field, it's too general.
- **Pick an outcome you can deliver.** "Double your sales" is a promise you can't keep and clients have learned to ignore. "Listings that answer buyers' questions" is believable.
- **Short beats clever.** If you need to explain a pun, drop it.
- **Use the subheading for the detail.** The headline gets attention; the line under it explains how.
- **Pattern 12 (question) works best when the answer is clearly "yes"** for your ideal client and "no" for everyone else.

## Subheading formula

> I [do what] for [whom] so [what changes], without [what they fear].

Examples:

- I write and edit help articles for software teams so support tickets go down, without your engineers having to write docs.
- I photograph small shops' products and spaces so your website and social posts look professional, without a big agency budget.
- I keep the books for freelance designers so tax time is a 20-minute job, without you learning accounting.

## Five-minute exercise

1. Write your client and outcome from `client-research.md` at the top of a page.
2. Write one headline for each of patterns 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6.
3. Cross out any that could belong to a competitor.
4. Read the survivors to a friend and ask: "Who is this for, and what do they get?" Keep the one they answer most accurately.
files.objection-faq.md:
# The Unasked Questions

Clients rarely email to ask "Are you going to disappear halfway through?" They just don't get in touch. A good FAQ answers those worries before they become a reason to leave the page.

Pick the four to six questions your clients worry about most (your `client-research.md` "fear" row will tell you). Answer each in two to four sentences, specifically and honestly.

## Money

**How much does it cost?**
> [Package] starts at [$X] for [what's included]. You'll get a fixed quote before you commit, and it only changes if you ask for something new.

**Why are you more expensive than [cheaper option]?**
> [Name what's different, specifically: you handle X, it includes Y, you've done it N times for businesses like theirs.] If [cheaper option] covers what you need, it might be the better choice, and I'm happy to say so on a call.

**Do I pay everything up front?**
> [Payment terms, e.g. "50% to book your start date, 50% on launch. For projects over $X, I split it into three payments."]

## Risk

**What if I don't like it?**
> [How feedback and revisions work: when they see work, how many rounds, what happens next.]

**What if you disappear halfway through?**
> [What protects them: you work with a written plan and dates; they own files/accounts from day one; you reply within N working days.]

**Who owns the work?**
> [What they own and when, e.g. "Once the final invoice is paid, everything is yours: files, accounts and passwords."]

## Effort

**How much of my time will this take?**
> [Honest estimate, e.g. "About two hours over four weeks: a kickoff call, two feedback sessions and the launch."]

**I'm not technical / creative / a writer. Is that a problem?**
> [Reassure with specifics: what you handle, what you'll guide them through.]

**What do you need from me to start?**
> [Short list: logo, access to X, a list of Y.]

## Fit

**Do you work with [type of client]?**
> [Yes, and an example of a similar project; or "My best work is with X. If you're Y, here's who I'd suggest looking for."]

**Can you also do [adjacent thing]?**
> [Yes, at what price; or no, and what you'd suggest instead.]

**How soon can you start?**
> [Current lead time, e.g. "I usually book 2 to 3 weeks ahead." Update this regularly, or say "Get in touch for my next start date."]

## Rules

- **Answer the question in the first sentence.** "How much?" gets a number first, explanation second.
- **Don't promise what you can't control.** Avoid guaranteeing rankings, sales, funding or results that depend on things outside your work.
- **Be willing to say "I'm not the right fit."** It makes every other answer more believable.
- **Keep it to six questions or fewer** on the page. Put the rest in your proposal or welcome pack.

files.review-checklist.md:
# Pre-Publish Checklist

Go through this with your draft open. Fix every "no" before you publish.

## Clarity (the first screen)

- [ ] The headline names a specific type of client.
- [ ] The headline names an outcome, not just a skill.
- [ ] The subheading says how you deliver it, in one sentence.
- [ ] There's one clear button above the fold on a phone.
- [ ] A stranger could say who this is for and what they get after five seconds (see the test below).

## The offer

- [ ] Two or three packages at most, with plain names.
- [ ] Each package says who it's for and what they get.
- [ ] Prices, "from" prices or a typical range are shown.
- [ ] Each package has a timeline.

## Trust

- [ ] The process section says what the client has to do and how long it takes.
- [ ] Every claim (numbers, results, client types) is true and you could back it up if asked.
- [ ] Testimonials, if any, are real, unedited and used with permission.
- [ ] The FAQ answers the biggest worries: cost, risk, effort and fit.

## Language

- [ ] Every phrase from `word-swaps.csv` has been replaced or justified.
- [ ] You say "I" if you work alone.
- [ ] No sentence is longer than about 25 words.
- [ ] Your clients' own words appear in the "Does this sound familiar?" section.

## Action

- [ ] The final section has one clear next step.
- [ ] It says when they'll hear back.
- [ ] The button or contact link works (test it on your phone).

## Practical

- [ ] The page reads well on a phone: short paragraphs, no tiny text, buttons easy to tap.

## The five-second test

Find someone who doesn't know your work well (a friend, a family member, a former colleague). Show them the top of the page on a phone for five seconds, then hide it and ask:

1. Who is this for?
2. What do they get?
3. What would you click?

If they can answer all three roughly the way you would, the top of your page works. If not, rewrite the headline and subheading and try someone else.

## The client test (optional, very useful)

Send the page to one past client you get on with:

> Hi [name], I've rewritten my services page and you're exactly who it's for. If you'd been reading this before we worked together, would anything have put you off or left you with a question? Two minutes of honest feedback would be really helpful.

The answer will usually point straight at a missing FAQ or an unclear price.

## Once a year

- Update prices and lead times.
- Swap in newer, better examples and testimonials.
- Re-run `client-research.md` if your best clients have changed.
